lesson.title: Measuring the Mind: From Mental Age to the Modern IQ Score
lesson.summary: Binet's original mental age concept and Stern's ratio IQ formula gave way to the deviation IQ scores used by modern intelligence tests.
lesson.body:
The idea of measuring intelligence with a single number has a specific historical origin. In the early 1900s, the French psychologist Alfred Binet, working with Theodore Simon, was asked by the French government to develop a practical way to identify schoolchildren who might need extra academic support. Binet's test was not designed as a measure of fixed, innate ability. It was designed as a practical tool, made up of a series of age graded tasks, to figure out whether a child's performance matched, lagged behind, or exceeded what was typical for children of their age.

This led to the concept of mental age, meaning the age level of intellectual performance a child's test results resembled, regardless of their actual chronological age. A seven year old who performed like a typical nine year old on Binet's tasks was said to have a mental age of nine. The German psychologist William Stern later proposed turning this relationship into a single ratio, the intelligence quotient, or IQ, calculated as mental age divided by chronological age and multiplied by one hundred. Under this formula, a child performing exactly at the level typical for their age would score exactly 100.

Binet's test crossed the Atlantic and was adapted by Lewis Terman at Stanford University, whose 1916 revision became known as the Stanford Binet Intelligence Scale and helped popularize IQ testing across the United States. This period of American testing history is also a caution about the misuse of psychological science: historians have documented that early IQ tests were sometimes applied in ways that are now considered ethically troubling, including being used to support discriminatory immigration restrictions and coercive eugenics era policies, well beyond Binet's original, more modest classroom purpose. This history is a reminder that even a scientifically grounded measurement tool can be misapplied when it is used to make sweeping judgments about groups of people rather than to help individuals.

The ratio IQ formula also has a practical flaw: mental age tends to level off in adulthood even though chronological age keeps increasing, which makes the simple ratio unreliable for adults. Modern intelligence tests, including current versions of the Wechsler scales, no longer use the mental age ratio at all. Instead they use what is called a deviation IQ, which compares a person's score to the scores of a large, representative standardization sample of people the same age, expressed on a normal, bell shaped distribution centered on a mean of 100. A score of 115 means a person performed better than most same aged peers in the standardization sample, not that they have some fixed mental age relative to their actual age.

Every modern IQ test, whatever its exact scoring method, is ultimately an attempt to operationalize the concept of general intelligence discussed in the previous chapter, turning the abstract idea of g into a concrete, standardized number that can be compared across individuals, and, as later chapters explore, across the standardized testing methods built on this same foundation.
